samples: This is a command-line to-do tool that keeps one task per line in a text file named todo.txt in the current directory. It can add a task from the words you type, remove a task by its 1-based number (so "done" deletes the task rather than marking it), or show the numbered list, and after an add or done it prints the updated list. Any unrecognized or malformed command prints a usage message, and a missing file is treated as an empty list. It needs console, environment and filesystem access, and the code does not say what happens if you give a number beyond the end of the list, so check that case before relying on it.

This is a command-line to-do tool that stores one task per line in a file called todo.txt in the current directory. Each run does one thing: add a task from the remaining words, remove the task at a given 1-based number (it deletes the task rather than marking it complete), or show the list. After an add or remove it saves the file and prints the numbered list, and anything unrecognized prints a usage line. It needs console, environment and filesystem access, and a missing file counts as an empty list. The program doesn't say what happens if you remove a number past the end of the list, so check that before relying on it.

This is a command-line to-do manager that keeps one task per line in a file called `todo.txt` in the current directory. It accepts "add" followed by the task words, "done" followed by a 1-based task number (which removes that task), and "show"; anything else prints a usage line, and after an add or done it saves the file and prints the numbered list. Before relying on it, note that a missing or unreadable file is silently treated as an empty list, so a later add would overwrite whatever the file held, and the code doesn't show what happens when the number given to "done" is larger than the list.

This is a command-line to-do tool that keeps one task per line in a file named todo.txt in the current directory. It accepts "add" followed by the task words, "done" followed by a 1-based item number to remove that item, or "show" to list the tasks; anything else, including a missing or invalid number, prints a usage message. Add and done save the file and then print the numbered list, but any read failure is treated as an empty list, so a file that exists but can't be read would be overwritten on the next add. The behavior when a done number is larger than the list isn't defined by anything I can see here.

This is a command-line to-do manager that keeps one task per line in a `todo.txt` file in the current directory. It runs one command per invocation: add a task (all remaining words become the task), mark a task done by its 1-based number (which removes it), or show the numbered list. Anything unrecognized, including a missing or non-numeric number, prints a usage message. A missing file is treated as an empty list, and after adding or completing a task it shows the updated list. The program only reads and writes that one file, and it prints to the console, so it needs no network access. The source does not say what happens when you mark done a number past the end of the list, so check that before relying on it.
